notes: A binary tree is a hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children: left and right.
explanation: A binary tree always has exactly two children.

notes: A binary tree is a hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children: left and right.
explanation: A binary tree has maximum of two children per node.

notes: BFS explores nodes level by level using a queue.
explanation: BFS uses a queue and visits nodes in layers.

notes: BFS explores nodes level by level using a queue.
explanation: BFS goes as deep as possible before coming back up.

notes: DFS explores as far as possible down each branch before backtracking.
explanation: DFS explores to the deepest level first.

notes: DFS explores as far as possible down each branch before backtracking.
explanation: DFS always guarantees the shortest path.

notes: The time complexity of binary search is O(log n).
explanation: Binary search cuts the search space in half every time, so it is O(log n).

notes: The time complexity of binary search is O(log n).

notes: In probability, independent events do not influence each other.
explanation: Independent events affect the probability of each other.

notes: In probability, independent events do not influence each other.
explanation: Independent events do not change each other's outcomes.

notes: OOP encapsulation hides internal details and exposes only necessary interfaces.
explanation: Encapsulation means wrapping data and methods while hiding internal implementation.

notes: OOP encapsulation hides internal details and exposes only necessary interfaces.

notes: QuickSort has an average time complexity of O(n log n).
explanation: QuickSort usually takes O(n log n) time to finish.

notes: QuickSort has an average time complexity of O(n log n).

notes: In a relational database, a primary key uniquely identifies each row.
explanation: A primary key is a column that uniquely identifies each record.

notes: In a relational database, a primary key uniquely identifies each row.

notes: A stack uses LIFO: last-in, first-out.
explanation: Stacks follow LIFO order.

notes: A stack uses LIFO: last-in, first-out.
explanation: Stacks follow FIFO order like queues.

notes: A queue uses FIFO: first-in, first-out.
explanation: Queues process items in the same order they arrive.

notes: A queue uses FIFO: first-in, first-out.
explanation: Queues remove the newest item first.

notes: Mergesort divides the list, sorts each half, and merges them back together.
explanation: Mergesort works by splitting the list and merging sorted halves.

notes: Mergesort divides the list, sorts each half, and merges them back together.
explanation: Mergesort swaps adjacent elements repeatedly.

notes: Hash tables use a hash function to map keys to indices in an array.
explanation: Hash tables rely on hashing to find the index for a key.

notes: Hash tables use a hash function to map keys to indices in an array.
explanation: Hash tables store elements in sorted order automatically.

notes: The worst case time complexity of QuickSort is O(n squared).
explanation: In the worst case QuickSort can degrade to O(n squared).

notes: The worst case time complexity of QuickSort is O(n squared).
explanation: QuickSort is always O(n log n) and never slower.

notes: Stable sorting algorithms keep equal elements in their original relative order.
explanation: A stable sort keeps equal items in the same order as the input.

notes: Stable sorting algorithms keep equal elements in their original relative order.
explanation: A stable sort always runs in constant time.

notes: Recursion must have a base case to stop the calls.
explanation: Without a base case, a recursive function will never terminate.

notes: Recursion must have a base case to stop the calls.
explanation: Recursion does not need any base case as long as you use loops.

notes: A linked list is a linear data structure where each node stores data and a reference to the next node.
explanation: A linked list stores each element with a pointer to the next element.

notes: A linked list is a linear data structure where each node stores data and a reference to the next node.
explanation: A linked list stores all elements contiguously in one big array.

notes: In big O notation, we focus on the dominant term and ignore constant factors.
explanation: Big O describes asymptotic growth and ignores constant multipliers.

notes: In big O notation, we focus on the dominant term and ignore constant factors.
explanation: Big O always gives the exact running time in seconds.

notes: A process is a running program with its own memory space, while threads share a process's memory.
explanation: Threads are lightweight units that share memory within a process.

notes: A process is a running program with its own memory space, while threads share a process's memory.
explanation: Threads always have completely separate memory spaces like different processes.

notes: Deadlock can occur when four conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
explanation: Deadlock needs those four conditions including circular wait.

notes: Deadlock can occur when four conditions hold: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.
explanation: Deadlock only happens when there is a single process using the CPU.

notes: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery of data, while UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery.
explanation: TCP is reliable and ordered, UDP is faster but unreliable.

notes: TCP provides reliable, ordered delivery of data, while UDP is connectionless and does not guarantee delivery.
explanation: UDP guarantees delivery but TCP does not.

notes: HTTP GET is typically used to request data, while POST is commonly used to send data to be processed.
explanation: GET usually fetches data and POST usually sends data to the server.

notes: HTTP GET is typically used to request data, while POST is commonly used to send data to be processed.
explanation: GET and POST are identical and can be used interchangeably without any difference.

notes: The derivative of a function at a point represents the instantaneous rate of change at that point.
explanation: The derivative tells you how fast the function is changing at a specific point.

notes: The derivative of a function at a point represents the instantaneous rate of change at that point.
explanation: The derivative always gives the total area under the curve.

notes: The definite integral of a function over an interval represents the signed area under the curve on that interval.
explanation: The definite integral gives the net area under the curve between the bounds.

notes: The definite integral of a function over an interval represents the signed area under the curve on that interval.
explanation: The definite integral always represents the slope of the tangent line.

notes: For matrix multiplication, the inner dimensions must match and the result has the outer dimensions.
explanation: To multiply matrices, the number of columns of the first must equal the number of rows of the second.

notes: For matrix multiplication, the inner dimensions must match and the result has the outer dimensions.
explanation: Any two matrices of any size can always be multiplied in any order.

notes: The normal distribution is symmetric, bell-shaped, and described by its mean and standard deviation.
explanation: A normal distribution is symmetric around the mean with most values near the mean.

notes: The normal distribution is symmetric, bell-shaped, and described by its mean and standard deviation.
explanation: A normal distribution is always skewed heavily to the right.

notes: The p-value in hypothesis testing is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
explanation: A small p-value means the observed data would be unlikely if the null hypothesis were true.

notes: The p-value in hypothesis testing is the probability of observing data at least as extreme as the sample, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
explanation: A large p-value always proves the null hypothesis is true.

notes: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on sample data.
explanation: A 95 percent confidence interval means we use a method that captures the true parameter 95 percent of the time in repeated samples.

notes: A confidence interval gives a range of plausible values for a population parameter based on sample data.
explanation: A 95 percent confidence interval means there is a 95 percent chance the already computed interval will change its endpoints.

notes: Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables but does not imply causation.
explanation: A high correlation does not prove that one variable causes changes in the other.

notes: Correlation measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables but does not imply causation.
explanation: If two variables are correlated, one must definitely cause the other.

notes: Overfitting in machine learning happens when a model learns noise in the training data and performs poorly on new data.
explanation: An overfitted model works very well on training data but generalizes badly to unseen data.

notes: Overfitting in machine learning happens when a model learns noise in the training data and performs poorly on new data.
explanation: Overfitting means the model is always simple and underestimates the patterns in the data.

notes: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that moves in the direction of the negative gradient to minimize a loss function.
explanation: Gradient descent updates parameters by moving opposite to the gradient to reduce loss.

notes: Gradient descent is an iterative optimization algorithm that moves in the direction of the negative gradient to minimize a loss function.
explanation: Gradient descent always jumps directly to the global minimum in a single step.

notes: In supervised learning, models are trained on labeled data consisting of input output pairs.
explanation: Supervised learning uses labeled examples where the correct answer is known.
